why/gpu: Training runs on GPUs, short for graphics processing units: chips first built to draw graphics, which do thousands of multiplications at once. Each has only so much memory.
why/fp32: As 32-bit numbers, four bytes each, a 7 billion parameter model's weights take twenty eight gigabytes of it.
why/half: In 16 bits, two bytes each, that halves to fourteen, and GPUs do 16-bit arithmetic several times faster.
why/catch: The catch: sixteen bits, each a zero or a one, can be set in only sixty five thousand five hundred and thirty six ways. So a 16-bit number has far fewer values to choose from.
float/sci: Which values? Scientists write a tiny number like this one as two times ten to the minus eight: a few digits, times a power of ten.
float/float: Change the power, and the point moves while the digits stay put: the point floats. Hence the name floating point numbers, or floats.
float/two: A computer stores them with powers of two: twelve is one point five times two cubed, one point five times eight.
float/mantissa: The digits, here one point five, are the mantissa: more bits for it keep more digits, more precision.
float/exponent: The power, here three, is the exponent: more bits for it reach bigger and tinier numbers, more range.
float/fp32: The standard 32-bit float, fp32, for floating point, gives one bit to the sign, eight to the exponent, and twenty three to the mantissa: about seven digits.
formats/bf16: Sixteen bits must give something up. bf16 keeps all eight exponent bits and cuts the mantissa to seven: fp32's whole range, but only about three digits.
formats/brain: The b is for Google Brain, the research group at Google where the format was conceived.
formats/fp16: fp16 keeps ten mantissa bits, so more digits, but only five exponent bits, so far less range.
formats/range: Above sixty five thousand five hundred and four, a number in fp16 becomes infinity, and below about six times ten to the minus eight, zero.
formats/fp8: And fp8 fits a number in a single byte.
master/grid: Now see what three digits cost. Near one, bf16 steps by about zero point zero zero eight: after one comes one point zero zero seven eight.
master/lost: Add an update of zero point zero zero zero one to a weight of one, and the sum rounds straight back to one: the update is lost.
master/copy: Paulius Micikevicius and colleagues, at NVIDIA and Baidu, fixed this in 2017: keep a 32-bit master copy of the weights, and take each step there.
master/fresh: Round that copy to 16 bits for the arithmetic. Small updates pile up in the master copy until, together, they move the 16-bit weight too.
master/name: Sixteen bits for the math, thirty two for the step: that mix is mixed precision.
scaling/tiny: fp16's range brought them a second problem. A gradient of two times ten to the minus eight, stored in fp16, becomes zero, and its weight stops learning.
scaling/scale: Their fix was loss scaling: multiply the loss by a large number, S, say one thousand and twenty four, before backprop. A constant factor carries through every derivative, so every gradient comes out S times larger.
scaling/safe: That gradient becomes about two times ten to the minus five, safely inside the range. Before the step, divide by S again, in 32 bits.
scaling/bf16: bf16 keeps fp32's eight exponent bits, so it reaches down to about ten to the minus thirty eight, and the same gradient survives with no scaling at all.
